title: The Places Beneath Earth's Surface You Won't Believe Exist
fullText: 1 kilometer beneath the mountains of Wajaka, Mexico, a team of cave divers is swimming through a flooded tunnel so narrow that their shoulders scrape both walls. Their air supply is calculated to the minute. The nearest exit is 14 hours behind them. The nearest hospital is 3 days away by mule. They have been underground for 26 days. Beneath the streets of Paris, in a section of tunnel that does not appear on any official map, 6 million human skulls and [music] femurss are stacked from floor to ceiling in walls that stretch for hundreds of meters. The bones have been there since the 1780s. Some of the tunnels that hold them have not been entered by anyone [music] with permission since Napoleon. In Turkey, eight levels of rooms descend into the earth beneath a [music] small town. kitchens, churches, stables, ventilation shafts, rolling stone doors designed to seal from the inside. 3,500 people [music] live down there. Nobody on the surface knew about it until 1963. And in Bise, inside a cave that the ancient Maya considered the entrance to Zebala, the underworld of the dead, a young woman's skeleton lies on the floor [music] of a chamber, untouched for over a thousand years. Her bones have fused [music] with the rock. They sparkle. She has been calcifying into crystal since before the Spanish arrived. And she is still there, glittering in the dark in the exact position she was placed [music] in when she died. These are the hidden places below the surface of the earth that were [music] never supposed to be found. Sealed, buried, flooded, forgotten, and every one of them was discovered by accident, by obsession, or by someone who refused to stop digging when the sensible thing to do was turn around. Before we start, drop a comment telling us where you are watching from right now. We want to see how many countries this video reaches. Number 15, Actun Tunichil Muknal, Kaio District, Bise. The entrance is a pool of water at the base of a limestone cliff in the jungle of western Bise. You swim through it. The water is chest deep and cold. After roughly 30 m, the cave opens into a dry passage. You walk, then wade, then swim again, then climb. After roughly 45 minutes, [music] you reach the main chamber and the floor is covered with the remains of the dead. Actun Tunichil Muknal, the cave of the stone sephiler was a Maya ceremonial site used between roughly 700 and 900 CE during the terminal classic period when Maya civilization was collapsing across the Yucatan. Research by archaeologist Haimeme A of Northern Arizona University has documented over 14 human skeletons inside the cave along [music] with hundreds of ceramic vessels, obsidian blades, and stone implements. The Maya [music] believed caves were entrances to Zebala, the underworld described in the Popalvu, a dark realm ruled by death gods. The people brought into this cave were offerings, sacrifices. The skeletons include adults and children. Some show signs of blunt force trauma to the skull. The most famous remains belong to a young woman roughly 18 years old at the time of death lying on her back in a chamber deep in the cave. Over the centuries, calsite saturated water has dripped onto her bones and fused them to the cave floor. The minerals have coated her skeleton in a thin layer of sparkling crystallin deposit. She is called the crystal maiden. In the beam of a headlamp, her bones glitter against the dark rock. She has been lying in the same position for over a thousand years. The calcification has made her unmovable. She is now part of [music] the cave. You cannot touch her. A rope barrier surrounds the site. Cameras have been banned since 2012 [music] after a tourist dropped one on a skull and shattered it. You can only stand in the dark in [music] a cave that the Maya believed was the entrance to the land of the dead. And look at a young woman who has been slowly turning into stone for 11 centuries. Number 14. Kaimaki underground city, Nevshir [music] Province, Turkey. In 1963, a resident of the small town of Kaimachi in central Turkey was renovating his home. He knocked through a wall in his basement. Behind it, a room he had never seen. Behind that room, a corridor. [music] Behind the corridor, another room and another and another. The rooms kept going downward [music] for eight levels. Kaimaki is one of over 200 underground cities carved into the soft volcanic tough of the Capidoshia region. Research by the Turkish [music] Ministry of Culture and Tourism has established that the underground complex extends to a depth of roughly 40 meters and could accommodate approximately 3,500 people. The layout includes living quarters, storage rooms for grain and oil, communal kitchens, ventilation shafts, water [music] wells, and a church with a nave and apps carved from the rock. The most remarkable defensive feature is the rolling stone doors. Circular stones roughly 1.5 m in diameter and 30 cm thick carved from single blocks of volcanic rock sit in recessed tracks inside the [music] corridors. From the inside, a single person can roll the stone into position, blocking the passage. The stone is too heavy [music] to push from the outside. The design turns every corridor into a lockable gate. Who built it is debated. Hittites, Friians, early Christians, and Byzantine era populations have all been proposed. The deepest levels show evidence of expansion over centuries. Different chisel marks, different room proportions, different ventilation techniques layered on top of each other. What is not debated is why every underground city in Capidoshia was built for the same reason, to hide. The Anatolian Plateau was a corridor for every invading army in history. Persians, Romans, Arabs, Mongols. The people of Capidoshia could not fight them, so they went underground. They rolled the stones shut. They waited in the dark. And when the army passed, they came back up. A city for 3,500 people, eight levels deep, stone doors that lock from the inside. Built by people whose survival strategy [music] for a thousand years, was to disappear beneath their own homes and wait for the danger to pass overhead. Number 13, the Paris Catacombs, Paris, France. There are two versions of the Paris Catacombs, the one tourists see [music] and the one they do not. The official tour covers roughly 1.5 km of tunnel beneath the 14th Aerandis Mall. Visitors descend 130 steps, walk past walls of neatly stacked skulls and femurss arranged in decorative patterns, and exit roughly 45 minutes later. The unofficial catacombs are 300 km long. They are unmapped in their entirety. They are illegal to enter and people enter them every night. The tunnels beneath Paris were originally limestone quaries mined from the Roman era through the 18th century to provide building stone for the city above. By the 1780s, [music] Paris had a problem. Its cemeteries were overflowing. The cemeterier deos in use for over 600 years had become a [music] public health crisis. Bodies were stacked in mass graves so shallow that the ground level of the cemetery had risen over 2 m above the surrounding streets. Basement walls of adjacent buildings were collapsing under the pressure of decomposing remains. [music] Between 1786 and 1788, the remains from the cemeterier deos and eventually from most of Paris's other cemeteries were exumed and transferred to the abandoned quarry tunnels. The bones of roughly 6 million [music] people were stacked in the tunnels in arrangements that were in some sections carefully organized by cemetery of origin and date of transfer. The illegal sections are where the story becomes stranger. The cataphiles, an underground subculture that has existed since at least the 1950s, [music] access the tunnels through maintenance hatches, metro connections, and entrances known only to those who have been shown. According to reporting by the Guardian and by French journalist Gil Tomas, who has documented the cataphile community extensively, the illegal tunnels contain art galleries painted on limestone walls, cinema rooms with projectors and seating carved from stone, bars stocked with wine, and at least one fully functioning [music] swimming pool fed by an underground stream. The police have a dedicated unit, the inspection general dear that patrols the tunnels. Fines for unauthorized entry are roughly €60. The cataphiles consider this the cost of admission. 6 million skeletons, 300 km of tunnel, an illegal subculture that has turned a mass grave into an art gallery, and a city of 2 million people living their lives directly above on streets paved with the same limestone that was quarried to create the tunnels that hold the bones of the people who walked those streets three centuries ago. Number 12, Cenote Anelita, Tulum, Kintanaroo, Mexico. Roughly 17 kilometers south of Tulum in the jungle of Mexico's Yucatan Peninsula, there is a cenote that contains something that should not exist. A river underwater. Cenote Anhalita is a circular sinkhole roughly 25 m in diameter. At the surface, the water is fresh and clear. Divers descend through it normally. At roughly 30 m depth, they hit a layer of mist. Below the mist, the water changes. It becomes darker, denser. And at the bottom of the cenote, at [music] roughly 60 m, there is a river. Not a current, a river [music] with banks, with a channel, with trees. The trees are dead branches and trunks that have fallen into the cenote over centuries and sunk to the bottom. The river [music] is a layer of hydrogen sulfide, a dense toxic gas dissolved in water that forms a distinct boundary separating the fresh water above from the salt water below. The boundary is so sharp that it looks like a riverbed. The hydrogen sulfide [music] layer flows slowly along the bottom of the cenote following the contour of the rock exactly like a river flowing through a landscape. Research published by cave diving biologist Sam Michechum of the Centro investigator delistma Aquifero de Kintanaro has documented that the hydrogen sulfide layer forms from the decomposition of organic matter that sinks to the bottom of the cenote. The salt water below and the fresh water above create a hallocline, a density boundary that traps the hydrogen sulfide in a visible band. Divers who descend through the hallline enter the river. Visibility drops to near zero inside the hydrogen sulfide layer. The gas is toxic at high concentrations. Below the layer in the salt water at the very bottom, visibility returns, [music] but the water is dark. The pressure is significant, and the sensation of having crossed through a river underwater and emerged into a different [music] world below it is, according to every diver who has done it, profoundly disorienting. A river at the bottom of a pool at the bottom of a hole in the jungle with dead trees along its banks in complete [music] darkness. The physics are understood. The experience is not something physics prepares you for. Number 11. Coochi tunnels, Ho Chi Min City, Vietnam. During the Vietnam War, roughly 250 km of handdug tunnels connected villages, supply depots, hospitals, [music] and command centers in the Coochi district northwest of Saigon. The Vietkong lived in them for years. The tunnels were dug by hand using short-handled hoes. The excavated earth was dispersed in rivers, bomb craters, and rice patties to avoid detection. The tunnel cross-section [music] was deliberately sized to accommodate Vietnamese fighters, but exclude the larger body frames of American soldiers. Research by Vietnamese military historians at the Coochi Historical Tunnel Museum has documented a three-level system. The first level, roughly 3 m deep, contained living quarters and fighting positions. The second level, roughly 6 m deep, held storage, kitchens, and meeting rooms. The third level, roughly 8 to 10 m deep, housed hospitals, weapons manufacturing workshops, and command posts. The kitchens were engineered to be invisible. Smoke from cooking fires was channeled through long, narrow tunnels and released through vents concealed in termite mounds or dense vegetation, dispersing the smoke over a wide area so that it was undetectable from the air. Water was drawn from underground wells. Air vents were disguised as antills. The US military became aware of the tunnels early in the war. Specialized units called tunnel rats, volunteer soldiers, typically small in stature, armed with a pistol, a flashlight, [music] and a knife, were sent into the tunnels to clear them. The mortality rate was extreme. Booby traps were placed at every turn. Sharpened bamboo stakes, tripwired grenades, and venomous snakes placed in bamboo tubes aimed at the tunnel ceiling. Despite carpet bombing, chemical defoliation with Agent Orange, and direct attempts to destroy the tunnels with explosives, the system remained operational throughout the war. The tunnels played a direct role in the 1968 Tet offensive when Vietkong forces launched coordinated attacks across South Vietnam using the tunnel network as staging areas. 250 km of tunnels dug by hand, hospitals underground, weapons factories underground, kitchens whose smoke came out of termite mounds, booby traps [music] that killed in the dark, and an army that lived beneath the feet of its enemy for years without being found. If you are still watching, hit subscribe. Tell us in the comments which hidden place has unsettled you the most so far. Number 10, Fingle's Cave, Isle of Stafa, Scotland. On the uninhabited island of Stafa in the inner Hebdes off Scotland's west coast, the ocean has [music] carved a cave into a cliff made entirely of hexagonal basaltt columns. The columns are so regular, so geometric, so precisely six-sided that they look engineered. They are not. Fingle's cave is roughly 70 m deep and 20 m high at the entrance. The basalt columns that form its walls, ceiling and floor are the result of a specific cooling pattern in volcanic lava. When basite lava cools slowly and uniformly, it contracts and fractures into polygonal columns, most commonly [music] hexagonal. The process called columnar jointing has been studied extensively by geologists since the 18th century. The cave's fame comes from its sound. The arched ceiling and the columnar walls create a natural acoustic chamber. Ocean waves entering the cave produce resonant tones that vary [music] with the wave size and tidal conditions. On calm days, the sound is a low rhythmic boom. On stormy days, it is a roar that echoes from deep inside the cave and carries across the water. In 1829, German composer Felix Mendelson visited Stafa by boat. The experience produced Deh Hebrdan, also known as Fingle's Cave Overture, one of the most celebrated orchestral works of the romantic era. Mendelson reportedly sketched the opening bars of the piece on the boat ride back from the island. The name comes from Finn Mcool Finn Mcool in English, the mythological Irish giant who, according to legend, built the giant's causeway in Northern Ireland as a bridge to Scotland. The Giant's Causeway roughly 130 km to the south is made of the same basaltt formations. The same lava flow, the same geological event split across two countries by millions of years of erosion and sea level change. A cave made of hexagons, carved by the ocean, tuned by geology, heard by a composer who turned it into music that has been performed for nearly 200 years. The cave is still there. Number nine, marble caves, General Carrera Lake, ice region, Chile. On the shore of General Carrera Lake, the second largest lake in South America in the Patagonian wilderness of southern Chile, water has spent roughly 6,000 years dissolving marble. The result is a series of caves, tunnels, and arches carved from solid white and blue marble that sits directly above the lake surface. The cave walls are swirled in patterns of white, gray, and deep blue. The water beneath them is turquoise. Light enters through the cave openings, bounces off the water, and illuminates [music] the marble from below, projecting rippling blue green reflections across the curved ceilings. The caves are accessible only by boat. No road reaches them directly. Visitors launch from the small town of Puerto Rio Tranilo and cross open water before entering the cave system by kayak or small motorboat. The lakes's color [music] changes with the seasons. Glacial meltwater in spring turns it pale turquoise. Summer warmth deepens it to cobalt. Geological analysis by the Chilean Geological Survey has established that the Marvel formations are part of a Paleozoic metamorphic complex dating to roughly 300 million years ago. The caves themselves were carved by wave action and chemical dissolution over the last 6,000 years as lake levels [music] fluctuated. The caves have no name in the indigenous Toelche language that has survived in the historical record. They were unknown outside of Patagonia until the early 2000s when improved road [music] access to Puerto Rio Tranilo. Caves carved by [music] 6,000 years of water. Light reflected upward through turquoise glacial meltwater onto swirled blue stone. And a location so remote that the road to reach it was not finished until 25 years ago. Number eight, [music] Ajanta Caves, Arangabad district, Maharashtra, India. In April 1819, a British officer named John Smith was hunting tiger in the forested ravines of the Siadri Hills [music] in western India. He looked across a horseshoe-shaped gorge and saw carved into the basalt cliff face the arched entrance of a cave. He crossed the river. He climbed the cliff. He entered the cave and found himself standing in a Buddhist prayer hall carved from living rock roughly 2,000 years earlier. The hall had a vated ceiling, columns with carved capitals and on the walls paintings. There are 30 caves at Ajanta carved into a cliff above the Wagora River between roughly the 2nd century B.CE and the 6th century CE. Research by the archaeological survey of India has classified them into two groups. earlier Hinayana caves, simple prayer halls and monastic cells, and later Mahayana caves, elaborate temples with [music] sculpture and painted murals. The paintings are what make Ajanta one of the most important archaeological sites on earth. The murals depict scenes from the life of the Buddha, from the Jatica tales, stories of the Buddha's previous lives, and from daily life in ancient [music] India. The colors are mineral-based pigments applied to dry plaster. Despite 1,500 years of exposure to humidity, insects, and bat colonies, [music] significant portions of the murals survive. Art historians have called the Ajanta paintings the finest surviving examples of ancient Indian art. Research by Benoy Bell, an Indian art historian and filmmaker who has spent decades photographing the caves using long exposure techniques, has revealed details invisible to the naked eye, subtle gradations of skin tone, expressions of sorrow and joy on faces smaller than a coin, and a mastery of perspective and forcehortening that would not appear in European art for another thousand years. The caves were abandoned around the 7th century [music] CE when Buddhist patronage in the region declined. The jungle grew over the cliff face. The entrances were hidden by vegetation. For roughly 1,200 years, nobody knew they were there. A tiger hunt, a British officer looking [music] across a gorge, and 30 caves filled with paintings that had been sitting in the dark unseen since before the Viking age. Number seven. Thrinuka, Gigor, Blafio, Iceland. Every volcano on Earth has a magma chamber. The chamber is where the molten rock sits before an eruption pushes it to the surface. After the eruption, the chamber empties. The walls are coated in cooled lava, and the chamber sits in the dark, deep inside the mountain, sealed and inaccessible. Thruka Gigor is the only volcano on Earth where the magma chamber is empty, intact, and open to human entry. The volcano last erupted roughly 4,000 years ago. The magma drained completely, leaving a chamber roughly 120 m deep and wide enough to fit the Statue of Liberty inside. The walls are coated in solidified lava in shades of red, orange, yellow, purple, and blue. The colors produced by different mineral compositions in the magma as it cooled at different rates. The chamber was discovered in 1974 by Icelandic cave explorer Arie B. Stefansson. He descended through the volcanic vent at the summit using ropes and climbing equipment. When he reached the bottom and looked up, he could see the circle of sky 120 m above him. a dot of light at the top of a cathedral of volcanic rock painted in every color the Earth's interior can produce. Since 2012, the chamber has been accessible to visitors [music] via a construction style open elevator that descends from the surface through the vent. The ride takes roughly 6 minutes. At the bottom, visitors stand on the solidified lava floor and [music] look up at walls that were liquid rock 4,000 years ago. Volcanologist Harolder Sigurson of the University of Rhode Island, who has studied three Nuka Gigor, has described it as the only place on Earth where a human can stand inside the plumbing system of a volcano and see [music] the internal structure that normally exists only in textbook diagrams. The only magma chamber on Earth you can walk into, 120 m deep, painted by cooling lava in colors that took 4,000 years to set. and a six-minute elevator ride from the Icelandic surface to the inside of a volcano. Number six, Mammoth Cave, Edmonson County, Kentucky, USA. Mammoth Cave is not the deepest cave on Earth. It is not the widest, it is the longest, and [music] it is not close. As of 2026, over 680 km of passageway have been surveyed inside Mammoth Cave. The second longest cave system [music] in the world, Jewel Cave in South Dakota has roughly 370 km. Mammoth is nearly twice [music] as long, and it is still growing. Not geologically, [music] but cardographically. Survey teams continued to discover new passages every year. The cave was known to pre-Colombian indigenous peoples for at least 4,000 years. Archaeological evidence documented by the National Park Service [music] includes reed torches, woven sandals, and the remains of miners who entered the cave to [music] extract gypsum and other minerals. In 1935, the mummified remains of a pre-Colombian minor were discovered beneath [music] a six-tonon boulder that had fallen on him roughly 2,000 years earlier. He was still holding a bundle of reeds. The cave became a commercial attraction in the early 1800s. During the War of 1812, it was mined for calcium [music] nitrate used in the manufacturer of gunpowder. In the mid 1800s, [music] enslaved people served as guides. Steven Bishop, an enslaved man who became the cave's most famous early explorer, is [music] credited with discovering many of the major passages. He drew the first accurate map of the cave [music] entirely from memory. The ecosystem inside Mammoth Cave includes over 130 species, many of them found nowhere else on Earth. The Kentucky cave shrimp, a small, blind, translucent crustation, is classified as endangered by the US Fish and Wildlife Service. It has no eyes. It has no pigmentation. It has been evolving in the cave system for millions of years. Research by the Cave Research Foundation, which coordinates exploration with the National Park Service, estimates that [music] between 400 and 600 km of additional passage may exist beyond the current survey limits. The cave is embedded in a limestone formation that extends across the entire region. Every time a survey team pushes through a tight passage or dives through a flooded section, they find more cave behind it. 680 km mapped, possibly over a thousand total. A minor crushed under a boulder 2,000 years ago, still holding his reads. A blind shrimp that has never seen the sun. And a cave that keeps going every time someone thinks they have found the end. Number five, Scotch John Caves, Dacha, Slovenia. The Reika River enters the limestone carst of southwestern Slovenia and disappears. It flows into a cave entrance and drops into the earth. Inside the cave, it is carved a canyon, not a passage, a canyon underground, 150 m deep, 120 m wide, [music] inside a mountain. The Scotch John caves are one of the most important cave systems on Earth from a scientific standpoint. UNESCO inscribed them in 1986, describing them as one of the most significant underground geomorphological sites in the world. The Reika River flows through the system for roughly 6 km underground before reemerging 34 km away at the Tamavo Springs on the coast of the Adriatic Sea near Trieste, Italy. The Martell [music] Chamber, named after French speliologist Edward Alfred Martell, who first explored it in 1890, is one of the largest underground chambers in Europe. Measurements by the Slovenian Academy of Sciences and Arts place it at roughly 308 m long, 123 m wide, and 146 m high. The Reika River flows across the floor of the chamber, 150 m below the walkway where visitors stand. The sound is what visitors describe [music] first. The river roars in the enclosed space of the underground canyon. The acoustics amplify every wave and every cascade. The sound fills the chamber [music] and bounces off walls that you cannot see in the darkness beyond the lights. Martell, who explored the cave in 1890 using ropes, candles, and a collapsible boat, described [music] the experience in his journals as standing at the edge of a world that human eyes were not designed to see. He wrote that the darkness beyond his candle light was not empty. It was full, full of sound, of water, of a space so large that his light could not find the walls. A river disappears into the earth. A canyon inside a mountain 150 m from the walkway to the water. And a sound that has been echoing off those walls since before anyone [music] was there to hear it. Number four, Orda Cave, Perm Cry, Russia. Beneath the western slopes of the Eural Mountains [music] in a gypsum carst formation near the town of Orda, there is a flooded cave system that holds water so clear that divers describe the sensation as flying rather than swimming. Orda cave is the longest surveyed underwater cave in Russia and the largest underwater gypsum cave in the world. Over 5 km of submerged passages have been mapped. The water temperature is a constant 4 to 5° Celsius year round. The visibility exceeds 45 m, farther than most divers [music] can see in any ocean. The clarity exists because the gypsum through which the water flows is chemically stable and produces almost no particulate. The water is filtered through kilometers of mineral before reaching the cave passages. There is no biological activity to cloud it. No algae, no sediment disturbance. The water is so transparent that divers have reported losing depth perception [music] entirely. The walls, floor, and ceiling visible simultaneously in every direction, creating a sensation of floating in a mineral cathedral with no up or down. Exploration of Orta cave has been conducted primarily by Russian cave diving teams, documented extensively by underwater photographer Victor Leaguskin, whose images have been published by National Geographic and the BBC. Leaguskin has described the experience of diving order as being inside a jewel. White gypsum walls and ceiling reflecting the divers's light in every direction. The Russian Geographical Society and the Perm Regional Government have limited diving to certified cave divers with specific cold water experience. The cave is not open to recreational diving. The clearest water on Earth inside a mountain of gypsum in the Euro Mountains of Russia. So transparent that divers forget they are underwater. So cold that the clock starts ticking the moment they enter. And so fragile that a careless fin can erase a millennium of geology. Number three, the Treasury interior, Petra, Jordan. Everyone has seen the Treasury, the rose red facade carved into the cliff face of a narrow canyon in southern Jordan. [music] Indiana Jones walked through the seek and saw it. Millions of tourists have photographed it. [music] It is the most recognizable archaeological monument in the Middle East. Almost nobody knows what is inside. Excavations led by Sammy Al- Nawaféle of the Petra Archaeological [music] Park beginning in 2003 revealed that the treasury was built on top of an earlier structure. The lower chambers [music] had been filled with sediment by flash floods over the centuries sealing them beneath the floor that visitors and archaeologists had been walking on for over a hundred years. The burial [music] goods had been looted in antiquity. But the architectural features, carved niches, prepared surfaces for sarcophagi and decorative elements confirmed the building'serary purpose. The [music] most famous facade in archaeology, photographed millions of times. And the actual tomb it was built [music] to protect was underneath the floor, sealed by mud, unknown until someone decided to dig down instead of looking up. Number two, the sacred cenote, Chichenita, Yucatan, Mexico. 60 m across, roughly 27 m from the rim to the water surface. Vertical limestone walls on all sides. No path down, no way to climb back up. The sacred cenote at Chichanita is a natural sinkhole that was the ritual center of one of the most powerful Maya cities in the Yucatan. And for over a thousand years, the Maya dropped things into it. valuables, offerings, people. [music] The offerings span roughly 800 years from the late classic period through the postclass and into the early Spanish colonial era. A hole in the limestone, 60 m across, over 200 bodies on the bottom, jade and gold broken on purpose and thrown into the dark.
